opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, and it's one I've been thinking about a lot lately. The basic intuition is that most of the uncertainty measures we use in computer vision come straight off the model's output: softmax confidence, entropy over the class distribution, maybe ensemble disagreement or Monte Carlo dropout. Those are useful, but they're fairly blind to meaning. If a model is torn between "husky" and "malamute," that's very different from being torn between "husky" and "fire hydrant," yet a flat softmax entropy can treat those two cases almost identically.

When the embedding space is semantically enriched, say aligned with language through something like CLIP-style training, or structured so that distances reflect real conceptual relationships, the geometry starts to carry meaning. Then you can ask richer questions. Where does this sample fall relative to the clusters of concepts the model knows? Is it sitting comfortably inside a well-populated region, or out in a sparse, ambiguous area between concepts? Is the model's confusion local and semantically sensible, or is it scattered across unrelated concepts, which usually means it's seeing something genuinely new?

That gives you a more interpretable notion of uncertainty. You can begin to separate "this is a hard fine-grained distinction" from "this input is out of distribution" from "this sample is probably mislabeled." Those have very different implications in practice. The first may be acceptable, the second is something you want to flag at deployment, and the third points back to a problem in your data.

That last point matters a lot to me, because I've come to believe so much of the leverage in computer vision is on the data side. If you can use semantically meaningful embeddings to find where your model is uncertain, and why, you can direct annotation effort, curate better training sets, find gaps in coverage, and catch label errors far more efficiently than by sampling at random. So for me, uncertainty isn't just a number attached to a prediction. Placed in a semantically rich space, it becomes a tool for understanding both the model and the data it learned from.

There are caveats, of course. The embedding is only as good as the data and supervision behind it, and language-aligned spaces carry their own biases. So you have to be careful not to treat the geometry as ground truth. But as a lens for reasoning about what a model does and doesn't know, I think it's a big step beyond raw confidence scores.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I've been thinking about for a long time, really going back to my academic work at Michigan and now with what we're doing at Voxel51. The core issue is that when we talk about uncertainty in vision models, most people reach for things like softmax confidence or maybe some ensemble disagreement, and those are fine, but they're really measures of the model's confidence in itself. They don't tell you much about whether the model is confused because the input is genuinely ambiguous, or because it's never seen anything like it, or because the label space is just poorly suited to what's in the image.

What a semantically enriched embedding space gives you is a way to ground those questions in structure. If your embedding space has been shaped so that distances actually mean something, say images of similar objects, similar scenes, similar lighting conditions cluster together, then you can start asking much more useful questions. Where does this sample sit relative to my training distribution? Is it in a dense region where I've got lots of support, or is it off in some sparse corner where the model is basically extrapolating? And crucially, when the model is uncertain, is it uncertain between semantically close things, like two breeds of dog, or between things that have no business being confused, like a dog and a stop sign? Those are very different kinds of uncertainty, and the second one is usually a signal that something is wrong with your data or your model, not just that the example is hard.

The other piece I'd emphasize is that these embedding spaces let you reason about uncertainty at the dataset level, not just one sample at a time. You can find regions where your labels are inconsistent, where annotators disagreed, where the model's errors concentrate. That's where a lot of the practical value is for teams building real systems. The model's uncertainty on a single image is interesting, but the pattern of uncertainty across the embedding space tells you what to go collect, what to relabel, and where your evaluation set is lying to you.

I'd add one caveat, which is that the enrichment matters a lot. If the embedding is just whatever falls out of the penultimate layer of your classifier, it inherits all of that model's blind spots. You get more robust uncertainty signals when the space is shaped by something broader, whether that's a foundation model, multimodal supervision, or explicit structure from the domain. So I think of it less as embeddings giving you uncertainty for free, and more as embeddings giving you a coordinate system where uncertainty becomes something you can actually inspect and act on.

astra-6.text:
I think they give us a way to ask a more meaningful question about uncertainty. Instead of just asking, “How confident is the model that this is a car?” we can ask, “What does this example look like relative to the concepts the model has learned?” Is it close to familiar examples? Is it between two concepts? Or is it far from anything we’ve seen before?

If the embedding space captures meaningful semantic relationships, those distinctions can help us separate ambiguity from unfamiliarity. An image might be ambiguous because two categories share visual characteristics, or it might be unfamiliar because it comes from a different environment. Those are different reasons for a model to be uncertain, and they may call for different responses.

The caveat is that distance in an embedding space isn’t automatically a calibrated measure of uncertainty. You still have to validate that relationship. But semantic structure gives us something richer to work with than a single confidence score—and potentially a better explanation of when and why the model needs help.

sol-6.1.text:
I think they give us a more meaningful way to ask what a model is uncertain about. A classifier can give you a confidence score, but that score doesn’t necessarily tell you whether the image is unfamiliar, whether two categories are genuinely ambiguous, or whether the model is relying on the wrong visual evidence.

If the embedding space captures semantic relationships, we can look at where an example sits relative to concepts and other examples. Is it close to a well-supported region? Is it between two related categories? Is it far from everything we’ve seen? Those are different situations, and ideally they should lead to different responses from the system.

The caveat is that distance in an embedding space isn’t automatically a calibrated measure of uncertainty. You still have to validate that relationship. But semantic structure gives you a basis for making uncertainty more interpretable—and potentially more useful for deciding when to ask a human for help.
